## What this tutorial builds

A **technical tariff** estimates expected claim cost before expenses, commission,
profit, taxes, and other commercial loadings. For policy \(i\):

- **exposure** is the insured time at risk and is the modelling weight;
- **frequency** is expected claims per exposure unit;
- **severity** is expected cost per claim, fitted only where claims occurred;
- **pure premium** is expected claim cost per exposure unit, either modelled
  directly or as frequency × severity.

Training rows contain rating features, exposure, and outcomes. Held-out evaluation
rows contain outcomes only so we can measure ranking and calibration honestly.
Production scoring rows need rating features and exposure, but no claim count or
claim amount.

This tutorial uses the French freMTPL2 portfolio because one dataset supports
direct Tweedie, frequency–severity, preprocessing, diagnostics, tariff export,
reporting, and experiment tracking. The
[Swedish motorcycle study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13385-021-00264-3)
is a useful methodological reference, but is narrower and is not duplicated as a
second tutorial.

## Setup and generated files

Install the Python environment with:

uv sync --group demo --extra mlops --extra plot

Quarto is an external system prerequisite. Render from the repository root with
`just demo`. Only this `.qmd` is source-controlled; every generated file goes
under `examples/_artifacts/fremtpl2/`, while the standalone HTML is ignored.

## Fetch, join, and clean pinned OpenML data

The frequency and severity datasets are pinned by OpenML data IDs
[41214](https://www.openml.org/d/41214) and
[41215](https://www.openml.org/d/41215). They are fetched through
`sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml`, following the
[scikit-learn insurance example](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_tweedie_regression_insurance_claims.html).
The source IDs and names below remain visible even when the joined Parquet cache
avoids another download.

Cleaning is deliberately deterministic and conservative:

1. cap individual claim amounts at 100,000 (large-loss stability; roughly a
   sixth of the uncapped total is removed and the tariff prices the retained
   layer);
2. aggregate severity rows to policy-level claim amount and left-join by
   policy ID;
3. retain unique policies with \(0 < exposure \le 1\), non-negative outcomes,
   positive density, plausible ages, bonus-malus in \([50, 230]\), vehicle
   power in \([2, 15]\), and consistent zero/positive claim count and amount;
4. rename only the columns used by Azoic and derive no outcome-informed
   features.

```{python}
source_metadata = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "openml_id": 41214,
            "name": "freMTPL2freq",
            "role": "policy exposure and claim counts",
            "source": "https://www.openml.org/d/41214",
        },
        {
            "openml_id": 41215,
            "name": "freMTPL2sev",
            "role": "individual claim amounts",
            "source": "https://www.openml.org/d/41215",
        },
    ]
)
display(source_metadata)
```

```{python}
if JOINED_PATH.exists():
    joined = pd.read_parquet(JOINED_PATH)
else:
    openml_cache = ARTIFACT_DIR / "openml-cache"
    frequency = fetch_openml(
        data_id=41214,
        as_frame=True,
        parser="auto",
        data_home=openml_cache,
    )
    severity = fetch_openml(
        data_id=41215,
        as_frame=True,
        parser="auto",
        data_home=openml_cache,
    )

    frequency_frame = frequency.frame.copy()
    severity_frame = severity.frame.copy()
    uncapped_total = severity_frame["ClaimAmount"].sum()
    severity_frame["ClaimAmount"] = severity_frame["ClaimAmount"].clip(upper=CLAIM_CAP)
    capped_total = severity_frame["ClaimAmount"].sum()
    claim_totals = (
        severity_frame.groupby("IDpol", observed=True, as_index=False)["ClaimAmount"]
        .sum()
    )
    joined = frequency_frame.merge(
        claim_totals,
        on="IDpol",
        how="left",
        validate="one_to_one",
    )
    joined["ClaimAmount"] = joined["ClaimAmount"].fillna(0.0)
    joined = joined.rename(
        columns={
            "IDpol": "policy_id",
            "Exposure": "exposure",
            "ClaimNb": "claim_count",
            "ClaimAmount": "claim_amount",
            "DrivAge": "driver_age",
            "VehAge": "vehicle_age",
            "BonusMalus": "bonus_malus",
            "Density": "density",
            "Region": "region",
            "VehBrand": "vehicle_brand",
            "VehPower": "veh_power",
            "VehGas": "veh_gas",
            "Area": "area",
        }
    )

    numeric_columns = [
        "policy_id",
        "exposure",
        "claim_count",
        "claim_amount",
        "driver_age",
        "vehicle_age",
        "bonus_malus",
        "density",
        "veh_power",
    ]
    joined[numeric_columns] = joined[numeric_columns].apply(pd.to_numeric)
    for column in ["region", "vehicle_brand", "veh_gas", "area"]:
        joined[column] = joined[column].astype("string").fillna("Missing").astype(str)

    consistent_outcomes = (
        ((joined["claim_count"] == 0) & (joined["claim_amount"] == 0))
        | ((joined["claim_count"] > 0) & (joined["claim_amount"] > 0))
    )
    valid = (
        joined["policy_id"].notna()
        & joined["policy_id"].duplicated(keep=False).eq(False)
        & joined["exposure"].gt(0)
        & joined["exposure"].le(1)
        & joined["claim_count"].ge(0)
        & joined["claim_amount"].ge(0)
        & joined["driver_age"].between(18, 100)
        & joined["vehicle_age"].between(0, 100)
        & joined["bonus_malus"].between(50, 230)
        & joined["veh_power"].between(2, 15)
        & joined["density"].gt(0)
        & consistent_outcomes
    )
    joined = joined.loc[
        valid,
        [
            "policy_id",
            "exposure",
            "claim_count",
            "claim_amount",
            "driver_age",
            "vehicle_age",
            "bonus_malus",
            "density",
            "region",
            "vehicle_brand",
            "veh_power",
            "veh_gas",
            "area",
        ],
    ].reset_index(drop=True)
    joined["veh_power"] = joined["veh_power"].astype("string").fillna("Missing").astype(str)
    joined.to_parquet(JOINED_PATH, index=False)
    print(
        f"claim cap at {CLAIM_CAP:,.0f}: removed "
        f"{1 - capped_total / uncapped_total:.1%} of the uncapped loss total"
    )

assert joined["policy_id"].is_unique
assert (joined["exposure"] > 0).all()
assert ((joined["claim_count"] > 0) == (joined["claim_amount"] > 0)).all()

portfolio = (
    joined.sample(
        n=min(SAMPLE_SIZE, len(joined)),
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
        replace=False,
    )
    .sort_values("policy_id")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
portfolio.to_parquet(PORTFOLIO_PATH, index=False)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "policies": [len(portfolio)],
        "exposure": [portfolio["exposure"].sum()],
        "claims": [portfolio["claim_count"].sum()],
        "claim_amount": [portfolio["claim_amount"].sum()],
        "observed_frequency": [
            portfolio["claim_count"].sum() / portfolio["exposure"].sum()
        ],
        "observed_pure_premium": [
            portfolio["claim_amount"].sum() / portfolio["exposure"].sum()
        ],
    }
)
```

## Descriptive review before learned preprocessing

Profiling and screening are descriptive review aids. They do not learn tariff
relativities and do not replace actuarial judgement. Binning and grouping below
are fitted later, using training rows only.

```{python}
features = [
    "driver_age",
    "vehicle_age",
    "bonus_malus",
    "density",
    "region",
    "vehicle_brand",
    "veh_power",
    "veh_gas",
    "area",
]
profile = profile_features(portfolio[features])
screening = screen_features(profile, max_groups=10, max_numeric_unique=20)
display(profile)
display(screening)
```

## Two reproducible experiments

freMTPL2 has no suitable policy-time field, so an out-of-time split would invent
an order that is not present. Both experiments therefore use the same fixed
random holdout (identical `random_state` and `test_size` on the same data), so
every model is scored on exactly the same test rows.

Every candidate receives `claim_amount / exposure` as its fit and score
target and predicts a pure-premium rate. `FrequencySeverityModel` also checks
that supplied rate against the aggregate outcome and exposure columns carried
inside `X`.

**Tariff-structured experiment.** Tree bins for driver age, vehicle age, bonus
malus, and density and similarity groups for region, vehicle brand, vehicle
power, vehicle gas, and area are learned on the training partition only.
Special outcome and weight columns remain available to supervised preprocessing
but are excluded from candidate features. Grouping relativities are
`sum(claim_amount) / sum(exposure)`, and `min_claims` is an aggregate
claim-count floor. Nominal levels are stably sorted by risk; ordered categories
keep their declared order. Under-credible groups merge with their closest-risk
neighbour, then the closest adjacent pairs merge until the group limit is met.
Each merge recomputes aggregate risk, with distance ties going left.

The **direct Tweedie GLM is the tariff baseline**. Its log-link model uses the
learned bins and groups as rating levels. The **raw-feature Tweedie GBM is the
flexible benchmark**. The **tariff-structured Tweedie GBM is the distillation
teacher**, using the same type of fitted structure as the GLM. These are roles,
not a validated model selection. All training parameters and the stored partition
are retained; we do not choose new cuts using this already-inspected holdout.

Frequency–severity fitting, comparison, and reporting are in the executable
appendix. Those models reuse the identical partition and existing settings.

```{python}
glm_config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="fremtpl2-tariff-structured",
    data_path=str(PORTFOLIO_PATH),
    spec=DatasetSpec(
        target="claim_amount",
        exposure="exposure",
        claim_count="claim_count",
    ),
    features=features,
    preprocessing=PreprocessingSpec(
        binner={
            "cols": ["driver_age", "vehicle_age", "bonus_malus", "density"],
            "strategy": "tree",
            "max_bins": 8,
            "min_exposure": 1000,
            "min_claims": 50,
            "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
        },
        grouper={
            "cols": ["region", "vehicle_brand", "veh_power", "veh_gas", "area"],
            "strategy": "similarity",
            "max_groups": 8,
            "min_exposure": 2000,
            "min_claims": 50,
        },
    ),
    split="random",
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    models={
        "direct-tweedie-glm": ModelSpec(
            kind="glm",
            params={
                "family": "tweedie",
                "link": "log",
                "tweedie_power": 1.5,
                "alpha": 0.001,
            },
        ),
        "tweedie-lightgbm-tariff": ModelSpec(
            kind="gbm",
            params={
                "objective": "tweedie",
                "tweedie_variance_power": 1.5,
                "n_estimators": 100,
                "num_leaves": 31,
                "learning_rate": 0.05,
                "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
            },
        ),
    },
)

gbm_config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="fremtpl2-raw-feature",
    data_path=str(PORTFOLIO_PATH),
    spec=glm_config.spec.model_copy(),
    features=features,
    split="random",
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    models={
        "tweedie-lightgbm": ModelSpec(
            kind="gbm",
            params={
                "objective": "tweedie",
                "tweedie_variance_power": 1.5,
                "n_estimators": 100,
                "num_leaves": 31,
                "learning_rate": 0.05,
                "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
            },
        ),
    },
)

display(pd.json_normalize(glm_config.model_dump(exclude_none=True)))
display(pd.json_normalize(gbm_config.model_dump(exclude_none=True)))
```

```{python}
glm_run, glm_estimators = run_experiment(glm_config, return_estimators=True)
gbm_run, gbm_estimators = run_experiment(gbm_config, return_estimators=True)
runs = [glm_run, gbm_run]
estimators = {**glm_estimators, **gbm_estimators}
assert set(glm_run.models) == set(glm_config.models)
assert set(gbm_run.models) == set(gbm_config.models)
assert glm_run.data_fingerprint == gbm_run.data_fingerprint
assert glm_run.train_indices == gbm_run.train_indices
assert glm_run.test_indices == gbm_run.test_indices
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(portfolio, pd.read_parquet(PORTFOLIO_PATH))

train_idx = np.asarray(glm_run.train_indices, dtype=int)
test_idx = np.asarray(glm_run.test_indices, dtype=int)
assert len(train_idx) == glm_run.n_train
assert len(test_idx) == glm_run.n_test
assert np.intersect1d(train_idx, test_idx).size == 0
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    np.sort(np.concatenate([train_idx, test_idx])), np.arange(len(portfolio))
)
```

The split happens before pipeline fitting, so the held-out outcomes cannot
influence the learned bins or groups. The returned positions identify the actual
random holdout; no second split is made. Positions refer to the exact input
frame in its original row order, not to index labels or policy IDs. The dataset
fingerprint and exact partition assertions above establish that both runs use
the same rows.

## Inspect the fitted tariff structure

These are **training-fitted candidates for review**. Exposure and claim-count
floors do not establish statistical certainty. Tree cuts may change across
samples. Similarity grouping uses loss rates before adjustment for other
predictors, so membership is not an adjusted causal effect.

```{python}
train_frame = portfolio.iloc[train_idx].copy()
pd.testing.assert_index_equal(
    train_frame.index, portfolio.index.take(glm_run.train_indices)
)
y_train = train_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_train = train_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()

raw_predict_columns = [*features, "exposure"]
special_predict_columns = [*features, "exposure", "claim_amount", "claim_count"]
```

```{python}
glm_pipeline = glm_estimators["direct-tweedie-glm"]
fitted_preprocessing = glm_pipeline[:-1]
fitted_binner = glm_pipeline.named_steps["binner"]
fitted_grouper = glm_pipeline.named_steps["grouper"]
bin_snapshot = {name: edges.copy() for name, edges in fitted_binner.mapping_.items()}
group_snapshot = {name: mapping.copy() for name, mapping in fitted_grouper.mapping_.items()}
train_grouped = fitted_preprocessing.transform(train_frame[special_predict_columns])
train_grouped[["claim_count", "claim_amount"]] = train_frame[["claim_count", "claim_amount"]]

for feature in features:
    grouped = train_grouped.groupby(feature, observed=True, sort=True, dropna=False)
    summary = grouped.agg(
        policies=("exposure", "size"), exposure=("exposure", "sum"),
        claim_count=("claim_count", "sum"), claim_amount=("claim_amount", "sum"),
    )
    summary["observed_pure_premium"] = summary.claim_amount / summary.exposure
    if feature in fitted_grouper.mapping_:
        mapping = fitted_grouper.mapping_[feature]
        summary["members"] = [
            ", ".join(str(level) for level, group in mapping.items() if group == label)
            for label in summary.index
        ]
    assert summary.policies.sum() == len(train_frame)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        summary[["exposure", "claim_count", "claim_amount"]].sum(),
        train_frame[["exposure", "claim_count", "claim_amount"]].sum(),
    )
    display(summary.reset_index())
```

Intervals are lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive at finite boundaries. The
following diagnostics reuse this fitted pipeline; they never refit the mappings.

## Held-out ranking, calibration, deviance, and lift

The reported Gini is a **concentration Gini for ranking only**, not a normalized
Gini. Equal prediction scores are aggregated into tied blocks, so row order inside
a tie cannot change the result. It does not establish calibration. O/P ratio,
exposure-weighted calibration deciles, and exposure-weighted mean Tweedie deviance
with fixed power 1.5 assess different aspects of fit and must be reviewed alongside
ranking.

Charts reuse the stored test positions. We calculate a training-only level
adjustment for every candidate before reviewing raw and adjusted holdout metrics.
The fitted estimators and their `Run` metrics remain raw.

### Measure calibration for every candidate

Write observed rate as $r_i$, predicted rate as $\mu_i$, and exposure as $w_i$.
Poisson, Gamma, and Tweedie deviances target conditional means; they do not
inherently target a rate below the mean. Model restrictions, regularization,
finite boosting iterations, and numerical convergence affect the achieved fit.
Neither the GLM label nor a Poisson GBM objective guarantees portfolio balance.

From [glum's deviance derivative and log-link definitions](https://glum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/glm.html),
$\partial d(r,\mu)/\partial\mu=2(\mu-r)/\mu^p$ and
$\partial\mu/\partial\beta_0=\mu$. Our derivation for a converged, unpenalized
log-link GLM with an intercept therefore gives

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_0}\sum_i w_i d(r_i,\mu_i)
=2\sum_i w_i(\mu_i-r_i)\mu_i^{1-p}=0.
$$

For Poisson ($p=1$), this implies training total balance,
$\sum_i w_i\mu_i=\sum_i w_i r_i$. For Gamma ($p=2$) and Tweedie
($1<p<2$), the extra prediction-dependent factor prevents that conclusion in
general. None of these training equations guarantees held-out balance, and
balance of a frequency component does not establish balance of a
frequency–severity product.

This small network-free example fits each family with just an intercept (the
feature is zero), then with one varying feature. Every intercept-only fit
recovers the exposure-weighted mean. The varying-feature Gamma and Tweedie
fits satisfy their intercept equations while their O/P ratios differ from one;
the Poisson fit is the control. The assertions allow solver error, rather than
requiring particular fitted totals.

```{python}
example_rate = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 8.0, 4.0])
example_exposure = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 3.0, 2.0])
balance_examples = []
for family, power in [("poisson", 1), ("tweedie", 1.5), ("gamma", 2)]:
    for varying in [False, True]:
        example_X = pd.DataFrame({
            "x": np.arange(-2.0, 3.0) if varying else np.zeros(5),
            "exposure": example_exposure,
        })
        example_model = RiskGLM(
            family=family, tweedie_power=power, link="log", alpha=0,
            exposure_col="exposure", gradient_tol=1e-9,
        ).fit(example_X, example_rate)
        example_prediction = example_model.predict(example_X)
        intercept_score = np.average(
            (example_prediction - example_rate) * example_prediction ** (1 - power),
            weights=example_exposure,
        )
        ratio = op_ratio(
            example_rate * example_exposure, example_prediction, example_exposure
        )
        assert abs(intercept_score) < 1e-8
        if not varying:
            np.testing.assert_allclose(
                example_prediction, np.average(example_rate, weights=example_exposure),
                rtol=1e-8,
            )
        if not varying or power == 1:
            assert np.isclose(ratio, 1, rtol=0, atol=1e-8)
        else:
            assert abs(ratio - 1) > 1e-3
        balance_examples.append({
            "family": family, "varying_feature": varying,
            "training_O/P": ratio, "mean_intercept_score": intercept_score,
        })
display(pd.DataFrame(balance_examples))
```

### Freeze a training burn-cost adjustment

For this tutorial, explicitly multiply **every** GLM and GBM candidate's rates
by its training observed/predicted ratio:

$$
c_m = \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathrm{train}}\mathrm{claim\ amount}_i}
            {\sum_{i\in\mathrm{train}}w_i\mu_{mi}},
\qquad \mu^{\mathrm{adjusted}}_{mi}=c_m\mu_{mi}.
$$

The factor uses the stored training positions only and is frozen before we
inspect holdout outcomes or metrics. It balances training totals; it need not
improve test deviance, test O/P, or segment calibration. A positive factor
preserves ranking while changing level diagnostics. The table shows training
O/P for all three main candidates and checks their adjusted training totals.

```{python}
recalibration_factors = {}
training_rows = []
for name, estimator in estimators.items():
    pred_train = np.asarray(estimator.predict(train_frame[raw_predict_columns]), dtype=float)
    assert np.isfinite(pred_train).all() and (pred_train > 0).all()
    factor = op_ratio(y_train, pred_train, w_train)
    assert np.isfinite(factor) and factor > 0
    recalibration_factors[name] = factor
    adjusted_op = op_ratio(y_train, factor * pred_train, w_train)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(adjusted_op, 1)
    training_rows.append({
        "model": name, "raw_training_O/P": factor,
        "frozen_factor": factor, "adjusted_training_O/P": adjusted_op,
    })
assert set(recalibration_factors) == set(estimators)
display(pd.DataFrame(training_rows))
```

### Charts on the held-out test rows

Re-predict every fitted model on the stored holdout using rating features and
exposure only, as in outcome-free scoring. Check raw metrics against each run,
then show raw and training-adjusted results on those same rows. The comparison
charts use adjusted predictions; the GLM structure illustrations explicitly use
raw rates. Model cards, comparison dashboards, and MLflow retain raw run metrics.

```{python}
test_frame = portfolio.iloc[test_idx].copy()
pd.testing.assert_index_equal(
    test_frame.index, portfolio.index.take(glm_run.test_indices)
)
assert not train_frame.index.isin(test_frame.index).any()
y_test = test_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_test = test_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()

raw_test_predictions: dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}
test_predictions: dict[str, np.ndarray] = {}
null_deviance = mean_tweedie_deviance(
    y_test / w_test,
    np.full(len(y_test), y_test.sum() / w_test.sum()),
    sample_weight=w_test,
    power=1.5,
)


def holdout_diagnostics(prediction):
    deviance = mean_tweedie_deviance(
        y_test / w_test, prediction, sample_weight=w_test, power=1.5
    )
    return {
        "gini_test": gini(y_test, prediction, w_test),
        "op_ratio_test": op_ratio(y_test, prediction, w_test),
        "deviance_test": deviance,
        "d2_test": 1 - deviance / null_deviance,
    }


holdout_rows = []
for name, estimator in estimators.items():
    prediction = np.asarray(estimator.predict(test_frame[raw_predict_columns]), dtype=float)
    assert np.isfinite(prediction).all() and (prediction > 0).all()
    raw_test_predictions[name] = prediction
    raw_metrics = holdout_diagnostics(prediction)
    result = (glm_run if name in glm_run.models else gbm_run).models[name]
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        list(raw_metrics.values()), [result.metrics[key] for key in raw_metrics]
    )
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(
        calibration_table(y_test, prediction, w_test, n_bins=10),
        result.calibration_table,
    )
    adjusted_prediction = prediction * recalibration_factors[name]
    test_predictions[name] = adjusted_prediction
    adjusted_metrics = holdout_diagnostics(adjusted_prediction)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(adjusted_metrics["gini_test"], raw_metrics["gini_test"])
    for scale, values in [("raw", raw_metrics), ("training O/P adjusted", adjusted_metrics)]:
        holdout_rows.append({"model": name, "prediction_scale": scale, **values})

holdout_metrics = pd.DataFrame(holdout_rows)
display(holdout_metrics)
metrics = comparison_table(runs).assign(prediction_scale="raw")
RAW_BENCHMARK = "tweedie-lightgbm"
BENCHMARK = "direct-tweedie-glm"
CHART_SCALE = "training O/P adjusted"
colors = model_colors(list(estimators))
```

from the concentration curve to the diagonal. A lower curve dominates another
only if it is nowhere above it; crossing curves do not establish dominance.

### Concentration Gini and inequality Gini

Azoic's prediction-ordered **concentration Gini** is

$$
G = 1 - 2\int_0^1 C(u)\,du
  = 2\int_0^1 \bigl(u-C(u)\bigr)\,du,
$$

where $u$ is cumulative exposure share and $C(u)$ is cumulative claim share,
ordered by increasing predicted rate. This is twice the **signed** area from
the curve to the diagonal: it can be negative, and positive area in one part
can offset negative area elsewhere. Zero Gini does not prove random ranking.
Azoic integrates tied-score blocks; its result equals the midrank formula,
but the implementation does not evaluate pairwise differences.

The pairwise absolute-difference **inequality Gini** instead measures dispersion
of observed rates independently of model predictions. Its exposure-weighted form is

$$
G_{\mathrm{ineq}}=
\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_iw_j|r_i-r_j|}
     {2(\sum_i w_i)(\sum_i w_i r_i)}.
$$

It equals the concentration Gini when the ordering score is the observed
rate itself. Reversing model predictions flips concentration Gini's sign and
leaves inequality Gini unchanged. With rates $[1,3]$ and exposures $[1,2]$,
claims are $[1,6]$ and the observed-rate curve passes through
$(0,0)$, $(1/3,1/7)$, $(1,1)$. Its two trapezoids have areas $1/42$ and
$8/21$: total $17/42$. Thus $G=2(1/2-17/42)=4/21$, not one even with
perfect observed-rate ordering.

```{python}
example_rate = np.array([1.0, 3.0])
example_exposure = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
example_claims = example_rate * example_exposure
inequality_gini = np.sum(
    example_exposure[:, None] * example_exposure[None, :]
    * abs(example_rate[:, None] - example_rate[None, :])
) / (2 * example_exposure.sum() * example_claims.sum())
example_curve = lorenz(example_claims, example_rate, example_exposure)
np.testing.assert_allclose(example_curve.exposure_pct, [0, 1 / 3, 1])
np.testing.assert_allclose(example_curve.claims_pct, [0, 1 / 7, 1])
np.testing.assert_allclose(example_curve.gini, 2 * (0.5 - 17 / 42))
for score, sign in [(example_rate, 1), (-example_rate, -1)]:
    np.testing.assert_allclose(gini(example_claims, score, example_exposure), sign * inequality_gini)
print(f"Inequality: {inequality_gini:.6f}; forward: {example_curve.gini:.6f}; "
      f"reversed: {gini(example_claims, -example_rate, example_exposure):.6f}")
```

Any strictly increasing transformation that preserves the prediction ties
preserves concentration Gini. In particular, the frozen positive training
factors leave ranking unchanged; the holdout table verifies this for all three main
models while showing the change in level diagnostics.

### Age one-ways: held-out calibration at each raw age

Start with driver and vehicle age on their original scales. Each point compares
observed claims per exposure unit with the exposure-weighted mean prediction for
held-out policies at that age. Exposure bars show the business supporting each
comparison; sparse ages can have noisy observed rates. These views can reveal
within-bin discrepancies that the grouped overview below averages away.

The predictions are the **raw direct GLM baseline**, without the training O/P
multiplier. The x-axis uses raw ages; the fitted model still uses its original
training bins. Other rating features and exposure composition change with age,
so average GLM predictions can vary even inside one fitted age bin. These are
portfolio comparisons, not isolated age effects or evidence of causality.

For individual conditional expectation (ICE) or partial dependence (PDP), use
scikit-learn's built-in `PartialDependenceDisplay` through the existing
[PDP/ICE recipe](https://thomasbury.github.io/azoic/guide/model-choice/#inspect-feature-effects-with-pdp-and-ice).
ICE varies one feature while keeping each row's other inputs fixed; PDP averages
those predictions. Neither curve measures observed segment calibration.

### Double-lift: raw GBM benchmark vs direct GLM baseline

A double-lift chart groups policies by the ratio of the raw-feature GBM
benchmark's prediction (A) to the direct GLM baseline's prediction (B). Both use their frozen
training adjustments here. Compare the gap between observed pure premium and
**each model's predicted pure premium within each ratio group**. Rising
observations alone cannot select a model. Extreme ratio groups contain the
largest relative disagreements and can be particularly informative, provided
their exposure and claims support credible comparisons; endpoints are not
constrained to match observations. The table below the small example reports
exposure and claim totals for the portfolio chart's ratio groups.

The [CAS GLM monograph, section 7.2.2, pp. 78–79](https://www.casact.org/sites/default/files/2021-01/05-Goldburd-Khare-Tevet.pdf#page=88)
uses this within-group comparison with curves normalized by their respective
portfolio averages. Azoic plots **absolute rates**, retaining level differences
as well as relative disagreement; it does not normalize those curves.

For example, observed rates and B both equal $[10,20,30]$, while A predicts
$[1,20,90]$. Observations rise with A/B, yet B matches every group and A has
errors of $[9,0,-60]$. Four repetitions per ratio keep all three quantile groups
in this small unit-exposure example.

```{python}
example_observed = np.repeat([10.0, 20.0, 30.0], 4)
example_a = np.repeat([1.0, 20.0, 90.0], 4)
example_double_lift = double_lift_table(
    example_observed, example_a, example_observed,
    n_bins=3, label_a="A", label_b="B",
)
np.testing.assert_allclose(example_double_lift.mean_ratio, [0.1, 1, 3])
np.testing.assert_allclose(example_double_lift.observed_pure_premium, [10, 20, 30])
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    example_double_lift.B_pure_premium, example_double_lift.observed_pure_premium
)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    example_double_lift.observed_pure_premium - example_double_lift.A_pure_premium,
    [9, 0, -60],
)
display(example_double_lift)
```

```{python}

    y_test,
    benchmark_pred,
    test_predictions[BENCHMARK],
    w_test,
    n_bins=10,
    label_a=RAW_BENCHMARK,
    label_b=BENCHMARK,
)
display(dl_table[["mean_ratio", "exposure", "claim_amount"]])
with azoic_style():
    plot_double_lift(
        dl_table,
        label_a=RAW_BENCHMARK,
        label_b=BENCHMARK,
        color_a=colors[RAW_BENCHMARK],
        color_b=colors[BENCHMARK],

        path=ARTIFACT_DIR / "double_lift.png",
    )
    plt.show()
```

### How to read these tables and charts

Four diagnostics answer four questions; a fifth (business sense) is checked by
humans, not the model. The full guide lives in the
[docs site](https://thomasbury.github.io/azoic/guide/actuarial-workflow/);
the condensed version used here:

- **Concentration Gini** measures prediction ordering, not premium level. A
  positive scalar leaves it unchanged. It is twice the signed area from the
  prediction-ordered curve to the diagonal and may be negative. Pairwise
  inequality Gini measures observed-rate dispersion; observed-rate ordering
  recovers that value. Azoic integrates tied-score blocks, equivalently
  the midrank formula, so row order within ties cannot affect the result.
- **Weighted deviance** is the proper score matched to the response distribution
  (Poisson for frequency, Gamma for severity, Tweedie for pure premium). Smaller
  is better; one unit does not translate directly to euros. When the true
  distribution differs from the assumed, deviance is a proxy for accuracy, not
  a measurement of it.
- **$D^2$** = $1 - \text{deviance}/\text{null deviance}$, the explained-deviance share against
  the weighted-mean null. Higher is better. $D^2$ is only comparable between models
  of the same response and same family; a frequency $D^2$ cannot be ranked against
  a severity $D^2$.
- **O/P (observed / predicted), also called A/E**, is $\sum_i w_i r_i / \sum_i w_i \mu_i$. A/E near 1 is necessary
  but not sufficient: a portfolio can hit 1.0 with offsetting biases that cancel
  across segments. Always segment-check (the one-way charts above are exactly
  that check).
- **Concentration curve** — Gini is twice the signed area to the diagonal. A
  lower curve dominates another only if it is nowhere above it; crossing
  curves do not establish dominance. The diagonal is the random-ranking
  reference and also results from constant prediction scores.
- **Lift chart** — observed and predicted per decile. The two should track on
  absolute level (calibration) and the observed should rise with the decile
  (ranking). Crossing signals that the model over-estimates in some deciles and
  under-estimates in others. The decile range is the rank-quality part; the
  gap between observed and predicted is the calibration part.
- **One-way chart** — the predicted lines should sit close to the observed line
  per feature level. A bowed observed line without a matching predicted line is
  systematic miscalibration by segment, not bad ranking.
- **Double-lift chart** — compare each predicted rate with observations within
  A/B ratio groups. Observed direction alone does not identify the better
  model. Extreme groups capture the largest relative disagreements; inspect
  their exposure and claims credibility. These are absolute-rate curves.
- **Hexbin (actual vs predicted)** — exposure density locates common outcomes,
  including the claim-free band at observed rate zero. The default scatter
  axes span their respective observed and predicted ranges, which can differ
  greatly when a few losses dominate the observed rates.
  A dense residual band need not estimate the conditional mean: zero-heavy
  outcomes often produce a band near $-\mu$ even for a well-calibrated model.

### Additive and multiplicative residual patterns

Residuals are observed rate minus predicted rate: $e_i=r_i-\mu_i$. Interpret
**credible, exposure-weighted grouped means** before attributing a pattern to
model structure. A constant non-zero conditional mean residual is an additive
discrepancy. If instead $r_i=c\mu_i$, then

$$
e_i=(c-1)\mu_i.
$$

That slope can be entirely multiplicative and removable by one factor. Remaining
curvature after checking level can motivate reviewing features, the link, or
interactions; density stripes alone do not diagnose their cause. Increasing
spread is compatible with Poisson, Gamma, and Tweedie variance and is not by
itself evidence of bias.

In the following deterministic grouped-mean examples, $r=\mu+5$ leaves residuals
$[5,5,5]$. Its portfolio O/P factor is 1.25, but applying it leaves
$[2.5,0,-2.5]$: one multiplier cannot generally remove an additive error.
For $r=2\mu$, residuals initially equal $\mu$ and multiplying predictions by
two removes every error.

```{python}
example_prediction = np.array([10.0, 20.0, 30.0])
example_exposure = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0])
for pattern, example_rate in [
    ("additive", example_prediction + 5),
    ("multiplicative", 2 * example_prediction),
]:
    factor = op_ratio(example_rate * example_exposure, example_prediction, example_exposure)
    residual = example_rate - example_prediction
    adjusted_residual = example_rate - factor * example_prediction
    np.testing.assert_allclose(residual, 5 if pattern == "additive" else example_prediction)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        adjusted_residual, [2.5, 0, -2.5] if pattern == "additive" else [0, 0, 0]
    )
    display(pd.DataFrame({
        "pattern": pattern, "prediction": example_prediction, "observed_rate": example_rate,
        "residual": residual, "factor": factor, "adjusted_residual": adjusted_residual,
    }))
```

For the adjusted working model, the calibration bins already provide grouped
mean residuals. Exposure and claim totals help assess how much evidence each
bin contains; this table does not estimate uncertainty.

```{python}
grouped_residuals = calibration_table(y_test, benchmark_pred, w_test, n_bins=10)
grouped_residuals["mean_rate_residual"] = (
    grouped_residuals.observed_pure_premium - grouped_residuals.predicted_pure_premium
)
grouped_residuals["prediction_scale"] = CHART_SCALE
display(grouped_residuals)
```

### The five-line checklist applied to these three models

- **Accuracy** — deviance and $D^2$ are smaller / larger than the GLM benchmark
  within the same family. The raw-feature GBM is the benchmark; the GLM is
  the within-family reference.
- **Portfolio calibration** — A/E near 1, with credible sub-segments. The
  one-way charts above check the direct GLM in its fitted groups. Compare other
  candidates in the same groups before making a segment-level choice.
- **Ranking** — positive Gini; the Lorenz curve dominates the GLM benchmark
  without crossing; positive-scalar invariance verified in the holdout table.
- **Lift** — observed per-decile tracks predicted in level; the decile range is
  large; no crossings of observed and predicted.
- **Business** — relativities make sense, fairness check passes, model is
  stable when re-fit on a resample (not shown here).

The verdict is the agreement of accuracy, calibration, ranking, and business
constraints — no single number makes a pricing decision.

## Score an outcome-free portfolio

The scoring interface remains `estimator.predict(raw_frame)`. No scoring
service or persistence layer is required. The frame below contains only rating
features and exposure. Every GLM and GBM rate shown is multiplied by its
frozen training O/P factor, matching the adjusted diagnostics above. Calling
`estimator.predict` alone returns raw rates.

```{python}
scoring_frame = portfolio[[*features, "exposure"]].copy()
scored = pd.DataFrame(index=scoring_frame.index)

for model_name, estimator in estimators.items():
    prediction = np.asarray(estimator.predict(scoring_frame), dtype=float)
    prediction = prediction * recalibration_factors[model_name]
    assert len(prediction) == len(scoring_frame)
    assert np.isfinite(prediction).all()
    assert (prediction >= 0).all()
    scored[model_name] = prediction

display(scored.describe().T.assign(prediction_scale=CHART_SCALE))
```

## Distil the GBM into an executable tariff

A tree model is not itself a multiplicative tariff. `distill_gbm` fits a
log-link GLM student to a GBM teacher's predictions on the experiment's
training rows, then measures fidelity on the untouched test rows. It copies the
already-fitted preprocessing, so bins and group mappings are not relearned from
the holdout. The teacher here is the **raw, unscaled tariff-structured** Tweedie
LightGBM (`tweedie-lightgbm-tariff`), before the chart adjustment: the student lives
in the same binned/grouped feature space. Fidelity measures agreement with this
teacher; it does not establish performance against claims.

The workbook contains the same `base_rate`, `factors`, and `mappings` sheets as
a direct GLM export. Here `recalibrate=False` is deliberate: applying the
workbook reproduces the student exactly. The student approximates the GBM
teacher; the workbook does not reproduce the teacher exactly. Export receives
only the training frame for feature metadata. The held-out fidelity metadata
still measures agreement with the teacher, not with claims.

```{python}
tariff_path = ARTIFACT_DIR / "distilled_tweedie_tariff.xlsx"
tariff_X = portfolio[
    [*features, "exposure", "claim_amount", "claim_count"]
]
teacher_pipeline = estimators["tweedie-lightgbm-tariff"]
fit_X = train_frame[special_predict_columns]
validation_X = test_frame[special_predict_columns]
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(fit_X, tariff_X.iloc[train_idx])
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(validation_X, tariff_X.iloc[test_idx])
distilled_pipeline = distill_gbm(teacher_pipeline, fit_X, validation_X)

export_tariff(
    distilled_pipeline,
    tariff_path,
    X=fit_X,
    recalibrate=False,
)

sheets = pd.read_excel(tariff_path, sheet_name=None)
assert list(sheets) == ["base_rate", "factors", "mappings"]
assert sheets["base_rate"].iloc[0]["distilled_from"] == "RiskGBM"
assert not sheets["base_rate"].iloc[0]["recalibrated"]
display(sheets["base_rate"])
display(sheets["factors"].head(20))
display(sheets["mappings"].head(20))
```

```{python}
factors = sheets["factors"]
numeric_factors = {}
categorical_factors = {}
for row in factors.itertuples(index=False):
    if row.level == "_per_unit":
        numeric_factors[row.feature] = float(np.log(row.multiplicative_factor))
    else:
        categorical_factors.setdefault(row.feature, {})[str(row.level)] = float(
            row.multiplicative_factor
        )

workbook_tariff = {
    "base_rate": float(sheets["base_rate"].iloc[0]["base_rate"]),
    "numeric": numeric_factors,
    "categorical": categorical_factors,
}
transformed_validation = distilled_pipeline[:-1].transform(validation_X)
teacher_rate = np.asarray(teacher_pipeline.predict(validation_X), dtype=float)
np.testing.assert_allclose(teacher_rate, raw_test_predictions["tweedie-lightgbm-tariff"])
student_rate = np.asarray(distilled_pipeline.predict(validation_X), dtype=float)
workbook_rate = apply_tariff(workbook_tariff, transformed_validation)

for frame in [fit_X, validation_X]:
    applied = apply_tariff(workbook_tariff, distilled_pipeline[:-1].transform(frame))
    student = np.asarray(distilled_pipeline.predict(frame), dtype=float)
    assert np.isfinite(applied).all() and (applied > 0).all()
    np.testing.assert_allclose(applied, student, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-8)
for step in ["binner", "grouper"]:
    original = teacher_pipeline.named_steps[step].mapping_
    copied = distilled_pipeline.named_steps[step].mapping_
    assert original.keys() == copied.keys()
    for name in original:
        if step == "binner":
            np.testing.assert_array_equal(original[name], copied[name])
        else:
            assert original[name] == copied[name]
```

### Teacher–student fidelity, separately from claims performance

Here the target is the **teacher's predicted rate**, not observed claims.
Weighted Tweedie deviance at power 1.5 is zero for exact reproduction; the
student/teacher predicted-total ratio is one for equal totals. Neither establishes
accuracy against losses or segment calibration.

```{python}
fidelity = {
    "teacher_student_deviance": mean_tweedie_deviance(
        teacher_rate, student_rate, sample_weight=w_test, power=1.5,
    ),
    "student_teacher_total_ratio": (student_rate @ w_test) / (teacher_rate @ w_test),
}
for key, value in fidelity.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value, distilled_pipeline.distillation_metrics_[key])
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value, sheets["base_rate"].iloc[0][key])
display(pd.DataFrame([fidelity]).assign(target="teacher rates", partition="test"))
```

### Four candidates against the same held-out claims

The applied workbook is the fourth candidate. Its rates come from the workbook
factors applied after the student's fitted preprocessing, not from a teacher
prediction. All four rows use exactly the same test claims and exposure.
Deviance is exposure-weighted Tweedie at power 1.5; $D^2$ uses the same constant
held-out mean reference as above. Concentration Gini measures ranking only.

The second table applies each candidate's **own frozen training O/P**. For the
workbook, compute that factor from applied workbook predictions on training rows;
it is an **external multiplier**, not a change to the exported base or factors.
It balances training totals and can improve or worsen held-out diagnostics.

```{python}
workbook_train_rate = apply_tariff(workbook_tariff, distilled_pipeline[:-1].transform(fit_X))
workbook_factor = op_ratio(y_train, workbook_train_rate, w_train)
assert np.isfinite(workbook_factor) and workbook_factor > 0
np.testing.assert_allclose(op_ratio(y_train, workbook_factor * workbook_train_rate, w_train), 1)
final_factors = {
    "Direct GLM": recalibration_factors["direct-tweedie-glm"],
    "Raw GBM": recalibration_factors["tweedie-lightgbm"],
    "Structured teacher": recalibration_factors["tweedie-lightgbm-tariff"],
    "Applied workbook": workbook_factor,
}
final_raw_predictions = {
    "Direct GLM": raw_test_predictions["direct-tweedie-glm"],
    "Raw GBM": raw_test_predictions["tweedie-lightgbm"],
    "Structured teacher": teacher_rate,
    "Applied workbook": workbook_rate,
}
final_adjusted_predictions = {
    name: prediction * final_factors[name] for name, prediction in final_raw_predictions.items()
}
final_rows = []
for scale, predictions in [("raw", final_raw_predictions),
                           ("training O/P adjusted", final_adjusted_predictions)]:
    for name, prediction in predictions.items():
        assert prediction.shape == y_test.shape
        assert np.isfinite(prediction).all() and (prediction > 0).all()
        values = holdout_diagnostics(prediction)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(values["gini_test"], gini(y_test, final_raw_predictions[name], w_test))
        np.testing.assert_allclose(
            values["op_ratio_test"], y_test.sum() / (prediction @ w_test),
        )
        final_rows.append({
            "model": name, "prediction_scale": scale, **values,
            "predicted_claim_amount": prediction @ w_test,
            "observed_claim_amount": y_test.sum(), "exposure": w_test.sum(),
            "frozen_training_factor": final_factors[name],
        })
final_metrics = pd.DataFrame(final_rows)
for scale in ["raw", "training O/P adjusted"]:
    table = final_metrics[final_metrics.prediction_scale == scale]
    assert len(table) == 4
    assert table.observed_claim_amount.nunique() == table.exposure.nunique() == 1
    display(table)
final_metrics.to_csv(ARTIFACT_DIR / "tariff_claims_comparison.csv", index=False)
```

### Calibration and ranking of the applied tariff

Each calibration panel compares observed and predicted rates in that candidate's
exposure-weighted prediction deciles. The diagonal means agreement in level.
The Lorenz overlay uses raw rates; positive training multipliers preserve every
curve, as checked above. Crossing curves do not establish ranking dominance.

```{python}
final_colors = model_colors(list(final_raw_predictions))
with azoic_style():
    for scale, predictions in [("raw", final_raw_predictions),
                               ("training O/P adjusted", final_adjusted_predictions)]:
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10), layout="constrained")
        for (name, prediction), ax in zip(predictions.items(), axes.flat, strict=True):
            table = calibration_table(y_test, prediction, w_test, n_bins=10)
            np.testing.assert_allclose(table.exposure.sum(), w_test.sum())
            np.testing.assert_allclose(table.claim_amount.sum(), y_test.sum())
            np.testing.assert_allclose(table.predicted_claim_amount.sum(), prediction @ w_test)
            plot_calibration(table, ax=ax, title=name)
        fig.suptitle(f"Four-candidate held-out calibration — {scale}")
        suffix = "raw" if scale == "raw" else "adjusted"
        fig.savefig(ARTIFACT_DIR / f"tariff_calibration_{suffix}.png", bbox_inches="tight")
        plt.close(fig)
        display(Image(filename=str(ARTIFACT_DIR / f"tariff_calibration_{suffix}.png"), width=700))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    plot_lorenz(y_test, final_raw_predictions, w_test, ax=ax, show_oracle=True,
                title="Four-candidate held-out Lorenz curves — raw rates")
    fig.savefig(ARTIFACT_DIR / "tariff_lorenz.png", bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)
    display(Image(filename=str(ARTIFACT_DIR / "tariff_lorenz.png"), width=700))
```

### Compare candidates at each raw age, then inside tariff bins

The first figure compares all four candidates at every observed driver and
vehicle age. Use it to locate differences that could be hidden by a fitted bin.
The second is a supporting tariff view using the direct GLM's frozen training
bins. This also puts the raw-feature GBM in those bins for reporting; it does not
alter its inputs or fit new cuts.

Both views reuse the same held-out predictions. Observed rates and exposure are
shared across candidates within each view. Raw and training O/P adjusted rates
appear in separate columns; "raw" in those column titles means no level
adjustment, independently of whether the x-axis uses raw ages or fitted bins.
These are portfolio averages, subject to composition and claim variation.
Read the sparse tails alongside exposure before interpreting a jagged line.

```{python}
with azoic_style():
    for grouping, frame, suffix in [
        ("each raw age", test_frame, "raw"),
        ("shared training bins", test_grouped, "grouped"),
    ]:
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(16, 13), layout="tight",
                                 gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1, 3, 1]})
        for row, feature in enumerate(["driver_age", "vehicle_age"]):
            for col, (scale, predictions) in enumerate([
                ("raw", final_raw_predictions),
                ("training O/P adjusted", final_adjusted_predictions),
            ]):
                ax, exposure_ax = axes[2 * row, col], axes[2 * row + 1, col]
                exposure_ax.sharex(ax)
                reference_table = None
                for name, prediction in predictions.items():
                    table = one_way_table(frame, feature, y_test, prediction, w_test, n_bins=None)
                    np.testing.assert_allclose(table.exposure.sum(), w_test.sum())
                    np.testing.assert_allclose(table.claim_amount.sum(), y_test.sum())
                    np.testing.assert_allclose(table.predicted_claim_amount.sum(), prediction @ w_test)
                    if suffix == "raw":
                        np.testing.assert_array_equal(table.level, np.sort(test_frame[feature].unique()))
                    common_columns = ["level", "level_label", "level_center", "exposure",
                                      "claim_amount", "observed_pure_premium"]
                    if reference_table is None:
                        reference_table = table
                        plot_one_way(table, ax=ax, color=final_colors[name], label=name,
                                     exposure="none", title=f"{feature} — {scale}")
                        exposure_ax.bar(ax.lines[0].get_xdata(),
                                        100 * table.exposure / w_test.sum(), color="lightgrey")
                        exposure_ax.set_ylabel("Exposure (%)")
                    else:
                        pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(table[common_columns], reference_table[common_columns])
                        ax.plot(ax.lines[0].get_xdata(), table.predicted_pure_premium,
                                marker="s", linestyle="--", color=final_colors[name], label=name)
                ax.set_title(f"{feature} — {scale}", y=1.02)
                ax.set_xlabel("")
                ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelbottom=False)
                exposure_ax.set_xlabel(f"{feature} (years)" if suffix == "raw" else "fitted training bin")
                ax.legend(fontsize=8)
        fig.suptitle(f"Held-out age comparisons — {grouping}, observed rates and exposure")
        figure_path = ARTIFACT_DIR / f"tariff_age_comparison_{suffix}.png"
        fig.savefig(figure_path, bbox_inches="tight")
        plt.close(fig)
        display(Image(filename=str(figure_path), width=700))
for name, edges in bin_snapshot.items():
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(fitted_binner.mapping_[name], edges)
assert fitted_grouper.mapping_ == group_snapshot
```

### What is gained and lost in this export?

The workbook gains a multiplicative factor representation. It preserves the
student's rates to the checked numerical tolerance, while approximating the
teacher's predictions. The table below reports **workbook minus comparator**
on claims: negative deviance differences mean lower loss; positive $D^2$ or
Gini differences mean improvement in that statistic. An O/P change must be read
against one, not maximized. Predicted-total changes are monetary level changes.

```{python}
export_differences = []
for scale in ["raw", "training O/P adjusted"]:
    table = final_metrics[final_metrics.prediction_scale == scale].set_index("model")
    for comparator in ["Direct GLM", "Raw GBM", "Structured teacher"]:
        columns = ["deviance_test", "d2_test", "gini_test", "op_ratio_test", "predicted_claim_amount"]
        differences = table.loc["Applied workbook", columns] - table.loc[comparator, columns]
        export_differences.append({"workbook_minus": comparator, "prediction_scale": scale,
                                   **differences.to_dict()})
display(pd.DataFrame(export_differences))
```

Distillation may improve or worsen claims performance: approximation error
against a teacher is not the same as prediction error against claims. Read the
differences alongside calibration and age panels; equal portfolio totals do not
imply equal segment rates. This single held-out split gives descriptive evidence,
not statistical superiority, stability under refitting, or an automatic choice
of production tariff. Adjusted workbook results describe the workbook **plus**
its external training multiplier; the exported workbook itself remains raw.

## Next steps: make premiums more stable

Sparse ages or vehicle categories can show large changes in predicted pure
premium because a small amount of data has too much influence. **Regularization**
means limiting how closely a model can follow those fluctuations. The aim is
to retain supported risk differences while reducing changes that depend on a
few policies or claims. A smoother-looking curve alone does not establish that
the premiums are better.

### Before fitting: pool sparse risks and limit model flexibility

Use the existing `PreprocessingSpec` and `ModelSpec.params` settings to compare
a few deliberate alternatives:

| Action in Azoic | What it can achieve | What it does not guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Increase `AutoBinner.min_exposure` or `min_claims`, or reduce `max_bins`. | Merge neighbouring age intervals so sparse tails share information with a larger group. The demo's 1,000 exposure units and 50 claims per bin are trial settings, not universal credibility thresholds. | Smooth transitions between bins, or enough evidence for every combination of rating factors. |
| Use the learned bins for a GBM as well as a GLM. | Prevent age distinctions inside a bin, holding other inputs fixed. The demo already includes this candidate as `tweedie-lightgbm-tariff`. | The best possible GBM: pooling can hide real differences, and other features can still split a bin into sparse leaves. |
| Increase `AutoGrouper.min_exposure` or `min_claims`, or reduce `max_groups`. | Pool sparse categorical levels, such as vehicle brands, using the configured grouping strategy. | Similar risk after accounting for other features: similarity grouping uses unadjusted loss rates. |
| Increase `RiskGLM.alpha`, keeping `l1_ratio=0` for an L2 penalty. | Pull fitted coefficients towards zero and temper extreme effects. | Similar factors for adjacent ages: the penalty does not connect neighbouring bins. |
| Reduce `RiskGBM.num_leaves`, set a smaller positive `max_depth`, increase `min_child_samples`, or increase `reg_lambda`. | Limit detailed interactions or shrink leaf estimates, making isolated fluctuations harder to fit. | A minimum exposure per leaf: `min_child_samples` controls observation support, not an exposure floor. |

If ages 80–95 share one bin, the model cannot use that age feature to charge an
otherwise identical 93-year-old differently from an 82-year-old. Bins create
flat steps with possible boundary jumps, not continuous curves. LightGBM's
internal histogram bins do not replace Azoic's exposure and claim-count floors.
See the [LightGBM regularization guidance](https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/stable/Parameters-Tuning.html).

Use a direction constraint only when the risk relationship supports it.
`RiskGBM.monotone_constraints` can require a numeric feature's predicted effect
to increase or decrease, holding other inputs fixed. Azoic rejects nonzero
constraints on categorical features, including `AutoBinner` interval categories.
Driver age need not have one direction across the whole age range.
`AutoBinner.monotonic` influences how training bins are merged; it does **not**
constrain the premiums subsequently fitted by the GLM or GBM.

### After fitting: distinguish shape changes from level changes

**First locate the instability.** Use `one_way_table` and `plot_one_way` to
inspect observed and predicted rates alongside exposure at raw ages and in
common training bins. Use the linked PDP/ICE recipe to inspect the fitted age
response while controlling the other inputs. Wider reporting groups make charts
less noisy but do not change any policy's prediction.

**Simplify a fitted GBM with `distill_gbm`.** This fits a multiplicative GLM to
the teacher's predictions and retains its fitted preprocessing. For this demo's
binned inputs, the student removes the teacher's flexible interactions. That
may improve stability, but can lose useful signal and retain uneven age factors.
Check performance against claims as well as agreement with the teacher;
distillation does not guarantee smoother or better premiums.

**Adjust the total when the overall level is wrong.** The training O/P multiplier
used above changes every rate by the same proportion. For a GLM tariff,
`export_tariff(..., recalibrate=True)` adjusts the exported base using supplied
outcomes and exposure; `recalibrate_for_total` returns an adjusted base for a
tariff dictionary. Estimate the adjustment on training or designated calibration
data and freeze it before evaluation. This corrects the total on those data,
not age-to-age swings or segment-level errors.

**Treat judgemental factor changes as a revised tariff.** `extract_tariff`
provides a GLM's factor dictionary; `apply_tariff` can score a revised copy on
the same preprocessed features. An actuary can replace selected categorical
factors there, then reassess totals and segment calibration. This is a manual
decision, not an automatic credibility or smoothing procedure. Record the
original factors and reasons for each change. Editing the dictionary does not
update the fitted model or a previously exported workbook. Changing bin
boundaries or group membership requires refitting the downstream model; do not
change a fitted pipeline's mappings and retain its old coefficients or trees.

### Check that stability has improved

Compare the raw-feature GBM, the binned GBM, and the simpler tariff on the same
validation rows. Review exposure-weighted Tweedie deviance, portfolio and
segment O/P, and age profiles. Refit on repeated training samples to see whether
tail premiums and learned boundaries move substantially; this tutorial does
not yet demonstrate that stability check. Relearn supervised bins and groups
within each training fold, and choose settings using validation inside the
outer training data. Keep the final test set for one evaluation. Since this
tutorial's holdout has already been inspected, further choices motivated by its
charts need fresh evaluation data.

Prefer the simpler candidate when predictive performance is comparable and
tail premiums are materially more stable. The evidence comes from these
comparisons, not from a smooth line or an exposure threshold alone.

## Reports and local MLflow tracking

Each experiment gets a Markdown model card and a standalone HTML comparison
dashboard; the cross-config comparison table collects the three main fitted models
from both experiments. These reports and MLflow metrics use raw run predictions,
before the training factors used in the adjusted comparisons and scoring example.

```{python}
glm_card_path = ARTIFACT_DIR / "model_card_tariff_structured.md"
gbm_card_path = ARTIFACT_DIR / "model_card_raw_feature.md"
dashboard_path = ARTIFACT_DIR / "comparison_dashboard.html"

glm_card_path.write_text(model_card(glm_run), encoding="utf-8")
gbm_card_path.write_text(model_card(gbm_run), encoding="utf-8")
dashboard_path.write_text(comparison_dashboard(runs), encoding="utf-8")

assert metrics["model"].nunique() == len(estimators)
assert glm_card_path.stat().st_size > 0
assert gbm_card_path.stat().st_size > 0
assert dashboard_path.stat().st_size > 0
display(metrics[["config", "model", "prediction_scale", "gini_test", "op_ratio_test", "deviance_test"]])
```

MLflow uses a local SQLite backend. Its artifact root is also placed under the
tutorial artifact directory. Each `log_run` call records the data fingerprint,
experiment and model parameters, all finite metrics, and the generated
artifacts.

```{python}
import mlflow

tracking_database = (ARTIFACT_DIR / "mlflow.db").resolve()
tracking_uri = f"sqlite:///{tracking_database}"
experiment_name = "azoic-fremtpl2-tutorial"
artifact_root = (ARTIFACT_DIR / "mlruns").resolve()

mlflow.set_tracking_uri(tracking_uri)
if mlflow.get_experiment_by_name(experiment_name) is None:
    mlflow.create_experiment(
        experiment_name,
        artifact_location=artifact_root.as_uri(),
    )

artifacts = [tariff_path, glm_card_path, gbm_card_path, dashboard_path]
mlflow_run_ids = [
    log_run(
        run,
        tracking_uri=tracking_uri,
        experiment_name=experiment_name,
        artifacts=artifacts,
    )
    for run in runs
]

client = mlflow.MlflowClient(tracking_uri=tracking_uri)
logged = [client.get_run(run_id) for run_id in mlflow_run_ids]

assert glm_run.data_fingerprint == gbm_run.data_fingerprint
assert all(
    entry.data.params["experiment.data_fingerprint"] == glm_run.data_fingerprint
    for entry in logged
)
assert all(
    f"{model_name}.gini_test" in entry.data.metrics
    for entry, run in zip(logged, runs, strict=True)
    for model_name in run.models
)
assert all(
    {Path(item.path).name for item in client.list_artifacts(run_id, path="artifacts")}
    == {Path(path).name for path in artifacts}
    for run_id in mlflow_run_ids
)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "run_id": mlflow_run_ids,
        "tracking_database": [str(tracking_database)] * len(mlflow_run_ids),
        "artifact_count": [len(artifacts)] * len(mlflow_run_ids),
    }
)
```

To inspect the run later, start the UI manually; rendering never starts a server:

```bash
uv run mlflow ui \
  --backend-store-uri sqlite:///examples/_artifacts/fremtpl2/mlflow.db
```

## Operational boundaries

This walkthrough produces fitted in-memory estimators and reproducible local
artifacts. It does **not** provide model persistence or deployment, expense or
profit loadings, a commercial premium, causal interpretations of associations,
remote MLflow, or a production scoring service. Claim outcomes are required for
training and evaluation, but not for scoring.

## Appendix: frequency–severity alternatives

These two alternatives use the same stored partition and unchanged model settings.
Frequency fits claim count / exposure with exposure weights. Severity fits
claim amount / claim count with claim-count weights on positive-claim rows only;
that filter remains inside `FrequencySeverityModel.fit`. Their product predicts
pure-premium rates. The GLMs use the tariff structure; the GBMs use raw features.

```{python}
fs_glm_config = glm_config.model_copy(update={
    "name": "fremtpl2-frequency-severity-glm",
    "models": {
        "frequency-severity-glm": ModelSpec(
            kind="frequency_severity",
            frequency=ModelSpec(
                kind="glm",
                params={"family": "poisson", "link": "log", "alpha": 0.001},
            ),
            severity=ModelSpec(
                kind="glm",
                params={"family": "gamma", "link": "log", "alpha": 0.001},
            ),
        ),
    },
})
fs_gbm_config = gbm_config.model_copy(update={
    "name": "fremtpl2-frequency-severity-gbm",
    "models": {
        "frequency-severity-gbm": ModelSpec(
            kind="frequency_severity",
            frequency=ModelSpec(
                kind="gbm",
                params={
                    "objective": "poisson",
                    "n_estimators": 100,
                    "num_leaves": 31,
                    "learning_rate": 0.05,
                    "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
                },
            ),
            severity=ModelSpec(
                kind="gbm",
                params={
                    "objective": "gamma",
                    "n_estimators": 100,
                    "num_leaves": 31,
                    "learning_rate": 0.05,
                    "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
                },
            ),
        ),
    },
})
appendix_runs = []
appendix_rows = []
for config in [fs_glm_config, fs_gbm_config]:
    run, fitted = run_experiment(config, return_estimators=True)
    assert run.data_fingerprint == glm_run.data_fingerprint
    assert run.train_indices == glm_run.train_indices
    assert run.test_indices == glm_run.test_indices
    appendix_runs.append(run)
    for name, estimator in fitted.items():
        train_prediction = np.asarray(estimator.predict(train_frame[raw_predict_columns]))
        prediction = np.asarray(estimator.predict(test_frame[raw_predict_columns]))
        assert np.isfinite(train_prediction).all() and (train_prediction > 0).all()
        assert np.isfinite(prediction).all() and (prediction > 0).all()
        raw_metrics = holdout_diagnostics(prediction)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(
            list(raw_metrics.values()), [run.models[name].metrics[k] for k in raw_metrics]
        )
        factor = op_ratio(y_train, train_prediction, w_train)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(op_ratio(y_train, factor * train_prediction, w_train), 1)
        adjusted = holdout_diagnostics(factor * prediction)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(adjusted["gini_test"], raw_metrics["gini_test"])
        for scale, values in [("raw", raw_metrics), ("training O/P adjusted", adjusted)]:
            appendix_rows.append({"model": name, "prediction_scale": scale,
                                  "training_factor": factor, **values})
    (ARTIFACT_DIR / f"{config.name}_card.md").write_text(model_card(run), encoding="utf-8")
    log_run(run, tracking_uri=tracking_uri, experiment_name=experiment_name)
display(pd.DataFrame(appendix_rows))
display(comparison_table([*runs, *appendix_runs]).assign(prediction_scale="raw"))
(ARTIFACT_DIR / "comparison_with_appendix.html").write_text(
    comparison_dashboard([*runs, *appendix_runs]), encoding="utf-8"
)
```

These are descriptive comparisons on one split, not evidence of statistical
superiority. All appendix reports and tracked metrics retain raw predictions.
